hints: Notice the two voltages are different: e.m.f. $12 \text{ V}$ and terminal p.d. $7.0 \text{ V}$ with internal resistance $0.10 \, \Omega$.
Recall that terminal p.d. is less than e.m.f. by the voltage lost across internal resistance: $V = E - Ir$.
Calculate the lost volts $E - V$ first, then divide that $5.0 \text{ V}$ drop by $0.10 \, \Omega$ to get the current in $\text{A}$.
walkthrough: Identify the given data: $E = 12 \text{ V}$, $r = 0.10 \, \Omega$ and terminal p.d. $V = 7.0 \text{ V}$ when supplying the starter motor.
State the governing relation for a source with internal resistance: $V = E - Ir$, where $Ir$ is the lost volts inside the battery.
Rearrange for current: $Ir = E - V$, so $I = (E - V)/r$.
Calculate and check units: $I = 50 \text{ A}$, a large but sensible starter-motor current.

options.A: Current gives lost volts of $12 - 7.0 = 5.0 \text{ V}$ across $0.10 \, \Omega$, so $I = 5.0/0.10 = 50 \text{ A}$.
options.B: This divides only the terminal p.d. by $r$, $7.0/0.10 = 70 \text{ A}$, ignoring that $r$ carries the lost volts $E-V$, not $V$.
options.C: This divides the full e.m.f. by $r$, $12/0.10 = 120 \text{ A}$, which would be the short-circuit current when $V = 0$.
options.D: This adds e.m.f. and terminal p.d., $(12+7.0)/0.10 = 190 \text{ A}$, instead of subtracting to find the voltage lost inside the battery.
